O Claude acabou de desvendar o bug. Era uma instrução cutomizada do instruction set (udf = user defined function). Que no caso dessa CPU a Matsushita implementou como um bit-search e o compilador usou na implementação de Huffman decoder, que faz parte do algoritmo de decodificar JPEG.

The JPEG decoder. With the display fixed, the splash showed *noise* instead of green — the software JPEG decoder was producing garbage. The cause was a single unimplemented CPU instruction: the MN10300/AM33 udf07 op (a bit-search, BSCH) used in the decoder's Huffman step. The CPU core was silently skipping it, desyncing the entire bit stream. Implementing it (bit position of the most-significant set bit) made the splash decode pixel-clean — verified against a reference decode of the same table-ROM JPEGs.

O mais doido foi que ele deduziu qual seria a função da instrução desconhecida. Pra fazer isso ele fez disasm do trecho problemático do código, percebeu qual era "a cara" do código, deduziu sua função, e concluiu qual seria a instrução exata necessária ali para que o assembly correspondesse a uma implementação válida de huffman decoding.

Teve também diversos momentos em que eu dei palpites usando minha intuição. Por exemplo, eu tava vendo ele desenhar bloquinhos enchendo a tela gradativamente. Me parece óbvio que isso não é algo que o usuário deveria ver, então palpitei: "tem alguma chance de estarmos renderizando pro usuário um offscreen buffer?"
E de fato era isso mesmo. Aí ele achou o outro endereço que é o front buffer e o resultado ficou melhor.

text.text: SB Mini II Is A Homebrew Apple II Clone

The SB Mini II is a homebrew clone of the original 1977 Apple II computer built using modern CMOS versions of the original ICs and including a Raspberry Pi Pico for USB keyboard support. It features SRAM instead of DRAM and a VGA output for a 3D-printed LCD monitor. The project is open source, with code and case files available on GitHub.

On the one hand, the original Apple II has been copied over and over again since at least the early 80s, so maybe this hack is old hat to the greybeards around here. On the other hand, this is the year 2026. When Apple released it back in 1977, who could have predicted people would still be building these things nearly five decades later?

texts.text: In that sense, a homebrew Apple II in the current year is pretty remarkable. It’s a really well done project by [simonboak],

text.text: nicely open sourced with a case to match

texts.text: , so is worth looking at on its own merits.
It doesn’t run
, but neither did the original.
is more this unit’s speed.

text.text: Unlike the later models, the original Apple II only used commercially available ICs, making it an easy target for recreation. No FPGAs required, just good old-fashioned DIPs. OK, these are modern CMOS versions of the chips, but other than that, the biggest concession to modernity is space on the board for a Raspberry Pi Pico to allow for connecting a USB keyboard.

texts.text: The

some other differences from 1977’s favorite home computer: SRAM vs DRAM — because you know the Woz would have used it if he could — and omitting the composite video circuitry in favor a late-model VGA card. There’s no need for the composite output since he’s eschewing the period-appropriate CRT for a retro-styled LCD monitor, which is also 3D printed and available on
. It’s crazy to think that the Apple II family lived long enough not only to see the dawn of VGA but also well into its sunset.

text.text: Fable 5: Does the smartest LLM decompile better?
I benchmarked Fable 5 against Sonnet 4.6 on 55 functions. It wins on the hard ones, but it costs 4x more

texts.text: We have a new model that everyone is talking about: Fable 5. Within the
community, there are mixed opinions about it. Some say it’s too expensive for little to no gain, while others say that it’s very helpful on the hardest functions.
In the
, I introduced
, a tool that guides LLMs to do
, along with a benchmark I ran with it. The dataset was 60 functions from two retro games. It used a leading model at the time: Claude Sonnet 4.6.

Matching decompilation is the art of converting assembly back into C source code that, when compiled, produces byte-for-byte identical machine code. It’s popular in the retro gaming community for recreating the source code of classic games. For example,
and

text.text: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time

texts.text: have been fully match-decompiled.
Well, I think it's good to have numbers™️ to guide this discussion. So,

text.text: let's run Mizuchi to benchmark Fable 5!

texts.text: Fable 5 is actually good, but a drop-in replacement might not be the right call.

text.text: The dataset is the same as in the previous benchmark. I really recommend reading the previous chapter for how the functions were picked, but in short: 30 functions from Sonic Advance 3 (SA3, a GBA game) and 30 from Animal Forest (AF, an N64 game).
One caveat for AF: 5 of its functions get matched without AI, solved by m2c in the programmatic phase. So, for measuring the model, AF effectively contributes 25 functions, not 30 like SA3.
Although the dataset is the same, the settings need adjusting because of Fable's token cost.

It stabilized almost all of Sonnet’s flaky matches.

texts.text: Run 1 confirmed that Fable introduced no regressions: the functions that Sonnet always matched still match on Fable, and except in one case, it got the best outcome:

text.text: if a Sonnet match is flaky, Fable likely stabilizes it, even with this stricter budget!
Under this strict budget, only one Sonnet-flaky function went unmatched by Fable in Run 1, and Fable even matched one extra function that Sonnet always failed to match.

On the gain side: beyond the one function Fable surprisingly matched back in Run 1, the larger budget in Runs 2 and 3 let it

How many functions match per attempt
In the previous benchmark using Sonnet, we learned that most functions match by the 3rd attempt, and few match on later retries.

texts.text: It's an even stronger statement for Fable, since

text.text: all matches happened within the first 3 attempts.

All the above results are great for Fable: more matches in fewer attempts. But now, let's talk about the main limitation: its cost.

Since Sonnet and Fable benchmark settings differ, we can only compare cost on the subset of data that’s equivalent across both runs. Then, I decided to compare the cost for matching a function that didn't hit the soft timeout.

texts.text: Using this data,

text.text: we can see that Fable is 3.5-4.6x more expensive than Sonnet in this case.

texts.text: It produces fewer output tokens, but these tokens are more expensive.

text.text: Microsoft Goes Nostalgic In Newest Open-Source Drop: Comic Chat Open-Sourced After 30 Years

Thirty years after its discontinuation, Microsoft has open-sourced the code for Comic Chat, the IRC client from Internet Explorer 3.0 released in 1996.
   •  The release preserves software history and allows the community to explore the original 1990s-era C++ and MFC code.
   •  Microsoft included experimental examples using AI tools to modernize the code for contemporary systems and high-resolution displays.
   •  The software is available under an MIT license on GitHub for experimentation and porting.

Introduced in 1996 with Internet Explorer 3.0, Microsoft Comic Chat provided comic-like avatars driven IRC chat client. After 30 years, this proprietary IRC chat client that was removed in Internet Explorer 6.0, is now open-source software. 

The most unexpected open-source code drop from Microsoft likely ever is today's open-sourcing of Comic Chat... What's next, Clippy? Comic Chat provided automatic illustrations of comic avatars for representing the IRC chat. Comic Chat was later renamed Microsoft Chat 2.0 but ultimately not all that important nor is it really useful these days with the software having been discontinued more than two decades ago. 

The biggest impact of Microsoft Comic Chat was that it ushered in the era of Microsoft's Comic Sans font. 

As for Microsoft's decision to open-source Comic Chat in 2026:

"By releasing Comic Chat as open source, we’re preserving an important piece of software history and giving the community an opportunity to explore, learn, and build upon it. 

The source is available now for exploration, study, and experimentation. Alongside the original snapshots, we’ve included a few AI-powered modernization attempts that demonstrate what’s possible—getting this 1990s-era C++ and MFC code building with current Visual Studio tools, connecting to modern IRC servers, and running legibly on today’s high-resolution Windows machines. These are not polished re-releases, but worked examples that show Comic Chat can still come alive on modern systems. We’re excited to see what improvements, ports, experiments, and entirely new forms the community brings to it next."
So now Microsoft engineers are even playing around with AI-powered modernization of 1990s era software...

text.text: Windows NT got its name from one of Intel’s failed x86 replacements

Windows NT got its name from Intel’s failed RISC processor, the i860, which was codenamed “N-Ten.” The i860 was intended to replace x86 but suffered from delays and poor performance. Microsoft originally developed NT for the i860 using a simulator, and the name “NT” stuck, even though the project later shifted to x86. Despite the i860's failure, its legacy lives on in the name of one of the world’s most popular operating systems.
Dave Farquhar published an article today about Windows NT 3.1’s place in the market when it was originally released, and while the article is interesting and a fun read, it does mention this:
[…] Microsoft took its nascent code that it intended to form the base of OS/2 3.0, renamed it Windows New Technology, and eventually released it as Windows NT 3.1.

texts.text: While Microsoft did, in fact, use the “New Technology” branding as a marketing trick, this is not what “NT” originally stood for. Two developers from the original Windows NT development team, Mark Lucovsky and David Thompson, explained
that “NT” came from the codename for Intel’s then-new RISC platform, the Intel i860 (Raymond Chen
of their story). The i860 was the first target platform for Windows NT, and it was codenamed “N-10” –

text.text: Finally, it was time to start writing some code. “We checked the first code pieces in around mid-December 1988,” Lucovsky said, “and had a very basic system kind of booting on a simulator of the Intel i860 (which was codenamed “N-Ten”) by January.” In fact, this is where NT actually got its name, Lucovsky revealed, adding that the “new technology” moniker was added after the fact in a rare spurt of product marketing by the original NT team members. “Originally, we were targeting NT to the Intel i860, a RISC processor that was horribly behind schedule. Because we didn’t have any i860 machines in-house to test on, we used an i860 simulator. That’s why we called it NT, because it worked on the ‘N-Ten.'”

texts.text: The

was one of Intel’s many attempts over the years to replace x86 with something more modern, but – as would become tradition with Intel and attempting to replace its x86 architecture – it suffered from endless delays, missed targets, and lacklustre performance. It saw only sporadic use in the market, and ended up on the chopping block after only a few years. Intel tried to replace x86 again soon after with Itanium, which suffered an identical fate.

text.text: Still, the engineers working on the i860 platform in the late ’80s and early ’90s at Intel can at least take some pride in that to this day, the most popular desktop operating system in the world got its name from the product they developed. Intel’s i860 might barely even be worthy of a footnote today, but billions of PC users log into their Windows “N-10” machines every day, unwittingly carrying a torch for the failed x86 replacement.

Our 'secret' project...

As you all know, we have 2 Aesthedes computers in the museum. Two incredibly rare machines where only 5 are known to exist today, and we have the only 2 functional ones. The Aesthedes is a CAD-computer with 6 screens and our version has 2x Motorola 68020 and 2x Motorola 68882 CPU. It was created in 1985.

[...]

We provided Enrico and Antonio with the ROMs, high res images of the board and all schematics so they can reverse engineer the system.

The video shows the emulator (in MAME) booting up the Aesthedes software. The top 2 screens are the output of the RS232 interfaces (directly from the CPU-cards) and the bottom 3 screens are the emulated data screens of the Aesthedes.
